\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{はくさい} (hakusai)}{はくさい (hakusai)}]{\ja{はくさい} (hakusai) — Chinese cabbage}

\label{lesson:JA-C114-hakusai}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a bonito, then the Japanese for wakame seaweed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{はくさい}}
\textbf{\ja{はくさい}} — \emph{hakusai} — \textquotedblleft{}Chinese cabbage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{はくさい}} (\emph{hakusai}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{haku}, \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{baek}) and \emph{sai}, \textquotedblleft{}vegetables\textquotedblright{} (\emph{tshojH}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{にんにく} (ninniku)}{にんにく (ninniku)}]{\ja{にんにく} (ninniku) — garlic}

\label{lesson:JA-C114-ninniku}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for wakame seaweed, then the Japanese for Chinese cabbage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{にんにく}}
\textbf{\ja{にんにく}} — \emph{ninniku} — \textquotedblleft{}garlic\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{にんにく}} (\emph{ninniku}) is written with characters for \textquotedblleft{}big\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}garlic\textquotedblright{}, read as a whole (JMdict). One account derives the word from a Buddhist term for enduring hardship; that is not settled. JMdict marks it as usually written in kana.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{あんこ} (anko)}{あんこ (anko)}]{\ja{あんこ} (anko) — sweet bean paste}

\label{lesson:JA-C114-anko}

Before the new one: say the Japanese for Chinese cabbage, then the Japanese for garlic.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あんこ}}
\textbf{\ja{あんこ}} — \emph{anko} — \textquotedblleft{}sweet bean paste\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あんこ}} (\emph{anko}) is Sino-Japanese \emph{an}, \textquotedblleft{}bean filling\textquotedblright{}, borrowed from Chinese in a later reading of its character, with the ending \emph{-ko} (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{はちみつ} (hachimitsu)}{はちみつ (hachimitsu)}]{\ja{はちみつ} (hachimitsu) — honey}

\label{lesson:JA-C114-hachimitsu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for garlic, then the Japanese for sweet bean paste.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{はちみつ}}
\textbf{\ja{はちみつ}} — \emph{hachimitsu} — \textquotedblleft{}honey\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{はちみつ}} (\emph{hachimitsu}) mixes the two layers: native \emph{hachi}, \textquotedblleft{}bee\textquotedblright{}, read as a kun'yomi, and \emph{mitsu}, \textquotedblleft{}honey\textquotedblright{}, the on'yomi of its second character, borrowed from Chinese (Middle Chinese \emph{mjit}; JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{あみ} (ami)}{あみ (ami)}]{\ja{あみ} (ami) — a net}

\label{lesson:JA-C114-ami}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for sweet bean paste, then the Japanese for honey.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あみ}}
\textbf{\ja{あみ}} — \emph{ami} — \textquotedblleft{}a net\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あみ}} (\emph{ami}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}
